stages.title: Finite element analysis
stages.hook: A computer predicts the stress in a bracket by splitting it into thousands of tiny pieces. Why does the answer sometimes change when the pieces are made smaller, and which answer should you trust?
explain: Finite element analysis (FEA) approximates a continuous structure by a mesh of simple elements joined at nodes. Each element has a stiffness relation between nodal forces and displacements. The solver assembles all of them into K u = F, applies supports (boundary conditions) and solves for the unknown displacements. Strains and stresses follow from the displacements.

The simplest element is a bar with stiffness k = A E ÷ L. For A = 100 mm² = 1 × 10⁻⁴ m², E = 200 GPa and L = 0.5 m, k = 4 × 10⁷ N/m, so a 10 kN load gives u = F ÷ k = 0.25 mm. Real models use shell and solid elements, but the principle is the same.

Results depend on the mesh, so a convergence study is essential: refine the mesh until the quantity of interest stops changing. Stress is less accurate than displacement, and at sharp re-entrant corners the theoretical stress is infinite (a singularity), so refining the mesh just keeps raising it. Real parts have fillets, so model them.

To judge yielding under multiaxial stress use the von Mises equivalent stress. For plane stress, σᵥₘ = √(σ₁² − σ₁σ₂ + σ₂²). With σ₁ = 100 MPa and σ₂ = 50 MPa, σᵥₘ = 86.6 MPa. Verification asks whether the equations were solved correctly (check against a hand calculation). Validation asks whether the model represents reality (compare with tests). A coloured plot is not evidence by itself.

example.q: A plane-stress point has principal stresses 100 MPa and 50 MPa. The material yields at 250 MPa. Find the von Mises stress and the safety factor against yield.

analogies.home: Tiling a curved bathtub with many small flat tiles: smaller tiles follow the curve better.

analogies.farm: Estimating a field's area by counting small squares: finer squares give a better estimate.

misc.wrong: A finer mesh always gives a more accurate stress.
misc.right: Refinement helps only where the model is physically sound. At singularities and wrong boundary conditions, a finer mesh gives larger but meaningless values.

stages.limits: FEA gives approximate answers that depend on element type, supports, loads and material models. Errors in the set-up can produce confident but wrong results.

questions.q: What equation does a linear static finite element solver assemble and solve?
o: K u = F
F = m a
P = T ω
σ = E ε only
questions.why: K is the global stiffness matrix, u the nodal displacements and F the load vector.

questions.q: A bar has A = 100 mm², E = 200 GPa and L = 0.5 m. What is its axial stiffness k = AE ÷ L in N/m? Give your answer in units of 10⁷ N/m.
A plane-stress point has principal stresses 120 MPa and 0 MPa. What is the von Mises stress in MPa?
questions.why: √(120² − 0 + 0) = 120 MPa: for uniaxial stress the von Mises stress equals the applied stress.

questions.q: A mesh is refined near a sharp internal corner and the peak stress keeps rising without limit. What does this indicate?
o: A stress singularity from unrealistic geometry
Perfect convergence to the true stress, so no change is needed
A faster solver in the software
A material error only, in the input data
questions.why: A perfectly sharp re-entrant corner has theoretically infinite stress, so the model needs a realistic fillet.

questions.q: Which activity checks that the FEA model matches physical reality?
o: Validation against tests
Verification of the solver only
Rendering colours
Refining the mesh
questions.why: Validation compares predictions with experiments. Verification checks the maths was solved correctly.

questions.q: An analyst fixes a part rigidly at the supports in a model, but in reality it rests on rubber pads. What is the likely result?
o: Stresses near the supports are overestimated or wrong
An exact match with the real part, since fixing is safer
Zero stress anywhere near the supports
Lower mesh quality only, with no effect on stress
questions.why: Boundary conditions strongly affect results, and rigid supports are stiffer than reality.

questions.q: A two-element mesh and a 200-element mesh give displacements of 0.249 mm and 0.250 mm for a simple bar. What does this suggest?
o: The displacement result is converged
The mesh is badly wrong because the two answers differ
The load must be zero in the model
Stress must also be wrong by a large amount
questions.why: Small change with refinement indicates convergence for that quantity.

questions.q: Why use von Mises stress instead of the largest principal stress for steel?
o: It predicts yield under combined stresses in ductile metals
It is always larger than the principal stress, so it is safer
It ignores shear and looks only at tension
It applies to brittle glass only and not to metals
questions.why: Yielding in ductile metals correlates with distortion energy.

questions.q: A colleague presents a bright stress plot and says the part is safe because no red areas appear. Give two checks you would ask for.
questions.model: I would ask for a mesh convergence study and for the boundary conditions and loads to be justified. I would also want a hand calculation or test to validate the result, and check the colour scale against the yield stress with a safety factor.
questions.why: Plots are only as reliable as the model and its checks.

questions.q: Match each FEA term to its role.
questions.why: These are the building blocks of an FEA workflow.

panel.q: A plate with a central hole has a nominal stress of 100 MPa and a stress concentration factor of about 3. What is the peak stress near the hole?
o: About 300 MPa
About 33 MPa
About 100 MPa
About 103 MPa
panel.why: σmax = Kt × σnom = 3 × 100 = 300 MPa, which may exceed yield locally.

panel.q: Which loading case needs a nonlinear analysis rather than a linear static one?
o: Large deflection or contact between parts
A small elastic bar pulled gently in tension
A stiff bracket under a small, steady load that barely moves it
A beam with a tiny elastic deflection only
panel.why: Contact, large deformation and plasticity make stiffness change during loading.

panel.q: A simulation is used to certify a lifting hook. What is the responsible approach?
o: Combine validated FEA with testing and code requirements
Rely on the colour plot, since it clearly shows the safe areas
Reduce the safety factor to match the model
Skip testing and save time
panel.why: Safety-critical decisions need independent validation, codes and margins.

teach.topic: How finite element analysis works and how far to trust it
teach.model: FEA splits a part into small elements joined at nodes. Each element has a known stiffness, and the computer solves K u = F for the displacements, then works out strains and stresses. The answer depends on the mesh, supports and loads, so you check convergence, compare with a hand calculation and validate with tests.

What does it solve?

Why shouldn't I just trust the picture?

stages.title: Computational fluid dynamics
stages.hook: A simulation of air around a car shows a neat smooth flow, yet a wind-tunnel test shows a swirling wake. Which is right, and what did the simulation leave out?
explain: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solves the equations of fluid flow numerically: conservation of mass, momentum (Navier–Stokes) and often energy. The flow domain is divided into small cells, and the equations are solved cell by cell for velocity, pressure and temperature.

The Reynolds number Re = ρ v D ÷ μ compares inertial and viscous effects. Water at 2 m/s in a 50 mm pipe (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, μ = 1 × 10⁻³ Pa s) has Re = 1 × 10⁵, which is turbulent, since pipe flow becomes turbulent above Re of about 4000. Air at 10 m/s over 0.1 m (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³, μ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ Pa s) has Re ≈ 66 700.

Turbulence has eddies over a huge range of sizes. Direct numerical simulation (DNS) resolves them all and is very costly. Large-eddy simulation (LES) resolves the large eddies and models the small. Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) models all turbulence with a model such as k–ε or k–ω SST, and is the most common in industry. Near walls, the mesh must resolve the boundary layer, judged by the dimensionless wall distance y⁺.

For time-dependent explicit schemes, stability needs a Courant number C = u Δt ÷ Δx below about 1. With u = 10 m/s, Δx = 0.01 m and Δt = 0.0005 s, C = 0.5. Good practice: check mesh independence, verify with simple cases, validate against experiments and state the model's limits. CFD can mislead if boundary conditions, turbulence models or mesh are poor.

example.q: Air (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³, μ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ Pa s) flows at 10 m/s past a 0.1 m body. Find the Reynolds number and say whether the flow is likely laminar or turbulent.
steps: Far above the transition range for most bodies, so the flow is likely turbulent.

analogies.home: Weather forecasts divide the atmosphere into grid cells, as CFD does.
analogies.city: Traffic simulations track vehicles in road cells with rules for flow and jams.
analogies.farm: Simulating how irrigation water spreads over a sloping field.
analogies.sea: Ship designers simulate flow around a hull to reduce drag before building.

stages.mnemonic: Mesh the fluid, set the physics, solve, then check against reality.

Averaged equations with a turbulence model for all eddies.
u Δt ÷ Δx, a stability and accuracy guide for time stepping.
Dimensionless distance of the first mesh cell from the wall.

misc.wrong: A converged CFD solution means the flow prediction is correct.
misc.right: Convergence means the equations are solved to a tolerance. The result may still be wrong if the model, mesh or boundary conditions are poor.

stages.limits: Turbulence models are approximations, and separated or transitional flow is hard to predict. Results need validation.

questions.q: What does the Reynolds number compare?
o: Inertial forces with viscous forces
Pressure with temperature in the fluid
Mass with length of the body
Speed of the flow with the speed of sound in it
questions.why: Re = ρ v D ÷ μ, the ratio of inertial to viscous effects.

questions.q: Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, μ = 0.001 Pa s) flows at 2 m/s in a 50 mm diameter pipe. What is the Reynolds number? Give your answer in thousands.
A flow solver uses u = 10 m/s, cell size Δx = 0.01 m and a time step Δt = 0.0005 s. What is the Courant number?
Which turbulence approach resolves the largest eddies and models the smallest?
o: Large-eddy simulation
RANS, which models all of the turbulence
DNS, which resolves every eddy down to the smallest
Laminar flow modelling with no eddies at all
questions.why: LES balances accuracy and cost.

questions.q: A simulation predicts attached flow but a test shows separation behind a car. What is a likely cause?
o: Turbulence model or mesh unable to capture separation
The car is not real, so no model can match it
The Reynolds number is zero in the test
Pressure is negative everywhere in the flow
questions.why: RANS models are weak for separated flow, and poor boundary layer meshing makes it worse.

questions.q: A CFD run was stopped when residuals fell below 10⁻³ but lift was still changing. What should the analyst do?
o: Monitor the physical quantity and run until it is steady
Accept the result, since residuals met the target
Stop at once and report the number
Ignore lift and watch only the residuals
questions.why: Residuals alone do not guarantee convergence of engineering quantities.

questions.q: A time step is doubled until the Courant number is 3 in an explicit solver. What is the likely outcome?
o: Instability or large errors
Better accuracy, since the steps are larger
Smaller cells in the mesh near the wall
No change in the result at all
questions.why: Explicit schemes need C near or below 1 for stability.

questions.q: Why is the first mesh cell near a wall made very thin in many RANS models?
o: To resolve the steep velocity gradient in the boundary layer
To reduce the cell count and save run time
To avoid walls in the flow
To increase the speed of the solver
questions.why: The wall layer controls drag and heat transfer, so it must be modelled well.

questions.q: List three steps that increase confidence in a CFD result before it is used for design.
questions.model: Check mesh independence, verify the solver against a simple known case, validate the model with experimental data and test the sensitivity to boundary conditions and the turbulence model.
questions.why: Confidence comes from verification and validation, not appearance.

questions.q: Match each term to what it measures or means.
pairs: Ratio of inertial to viscous effects
questions.why: These terms organise CFD choices.

panel.q: A model of a small drone propeller needs fine mesh near the blade. Why not use that mesh density everywhere?
o: Cost grows greatly, so refine only where gradients are large
Fine meshes are illegal in published work
Coarse meshes are always exact
It does not matter where the cells are placed
panel.why: Adaptive or local refinement saves computing effort.

panel.q: If a wind-tunnel test and a CFD run disagree by 20% on drag, what is the best engineering response?
o: Investigate both the test and the model for errors
Trust CFD always, since the computer is precise
Trust tests always, since the model is only a guess
Ignore both results and use a rule of thumb
panel.why: Both can have errors, such as blockage in the tunnel or model error in CFD.

panel.q: Why is CFD of a building fire smoke spread safety-relevant?
o: It informs escape and ventilation design but needs validation
It replaces fire codes with a simple picture
It removes the need for fire exits in the building
It is always exact and needs no checking
panel.why: Simulation helps compare options, but results must be validated and used with codes.

teach.topic: What CFD does and why results need checking
teach.model: CFD splits the fluid into small cells and solves the equations for mass, momentum and energy in each. Turbulence is usually modelled, not resolved, which adds error. A run that has converged is not necessarily right, so engineers check the mesh, verify against simple cases and validate with experiments.

points.ask: What does the software do to the flow region?
What does it solve in each cell?
What is the hard part?
How do you know the result is right?

stages.title: Fatigue and fracture mechanics
stages.hook: A steel axle carried its normal load for years, far below its yield strength, then snapped without warning. What was happening inside it all that time?
explain: Fatigue is damage from repeated loading. A crack starts at a stress concentration such as a keyway, hole, scratch or weld toe, grows a tiny amount each cycle and finally the remaining section fails suddenly. Fatigue failures often show beach marks on the fracture face. Fatigue is a leading cause of failure of rotating and vibrating machinery.

The S–N curve plots stress amplitude against cycles to failure. Many steels have an endurance limit Se below which life is effectively infinite; aluminium does not, so a fatigue strength at a stated life (for example 10⁷ cycles) is used. Mean stress reduces allowable amplitude. The Goodman relation gives σₐ ÷ Se + σₘ ÷ Sᵤ = 1 ÷ n. With σₐ = 100 MPa, σₘ = 100 MPa, Se = 250 MPa and Sᵤ = 500 MPa: 0.4 + 0.2 = 0.6, so n = 1.67.

Miner's rule adds damage from different stress blocks: D = Σ nᵢ ÷ Nᵢ, with failure predicted at D = 1. 20 000 cycles where life is 100 000 contribute 0.2, and 50 000 cycles where life is 500 000 contribute 0.1, so D = 0.3.

Fracture mechanics treats the crack. The stress intensity factor is K = Y σ √(π a). Fracture occurs when K reaches the toughness Kᵢc. For σ = 100 MPa, a = 5 mm and Y = 1: K = 12.5 MPa√m. With Kᵢc = 50 MPa√m, the critical crack length is a_c = (1 ÷ π)(50 ÷ 100)² = 0.0796 m = 79.6 mm. Design responses: lower stress, add fillets, polish or shot-peen surfaces, choose tough materials and inspect on a schedule so cracks are found long before critical size.

example.q: A part has a 5 mm edge crack in a plate under 100 MPa stress. Using K = σ√(π a) with Y = 1, find K. If Kᵢc = 50 MPa√m, find the critical crack length.
steps: Critical: K = Kᵢc, so a_c = (1 ÷ π)(Kᵢc ÷ σ)².

analogies.home: Bending a paper clip back and forth breaks it far below the force that would snap it in one go.
analogies.city: A bridge deck bears millions of vehicle passes. Tiny cracks can grow over years.

analogies.sea: Ship hulls flex with waves, so cracks may start at hatch corners.

Crack-tip loading measure, Y σ √(π a).
The critical K at which a crack grows unstably.

misc.wrong: If the stress is below yield, the part will last forever.
misc.right: Repeated stress below yield can still grow cracks and cause failure, especially at stress concentrations.

stages.limits: Fatigue life has large scatter, and effects such as corrosion, surface finish, size and temperature must be applied as correction factors.

questions.q: Where do fatigue cracks usually start?
o: At stress concentrations like notches, holes and weld toes
At the smoothest, most polished part of the surface
At the neutral centre of the part
At the exact middle of a bar, far from the surface
questions.why: Local stress is highest there.

questions.q: A load cycles between σmax = 200 MPa and σmin = 0. What is the stress amplitude in MPa?
Using Goodman with σa = 100 MPa, σm = 100 MPa, Se = 250 MPa and Su = 500 MPa, what is the fatigue safety factor n?
A part sees 20 000 cycles at a level where life is 100 000 cycles, and 50 000 cycles at a level where life is 500 000. Using Miner's rule, what is the damage sum D?
A crack in a plate grows from 5 mm to 10 mm at the same stress. What happens to K?
o: It rises by a factor of √2
It doubles, in step with the crack length
It halves as the crack gets longer
It does not change at the same stress
questions.why: K ∝ √a, so doubling a multiplies K by about 1.41.

questions.q: Which action most directly lengthens fatigue life of a shaft with a shoulder?
o: Add a generous fillet radius at the shoulder
Sharpen the shoulder to a tight corner
Add scratches to the surface for grip
Increase the vibration on the shaft
questions.why: A larger radius reduces the stress concentration factor.

questions.q: A fracture surface shows beach marks and a small final rough zone. What does this indicate?
o: Fatigue growth under low nominal stress
Overload at once from a single large force
Corrosion only, with no cyclic loading
A casting error only, from the time of manufacture
questions.why: A small final zone means the stress was low and the crack grew large before failure.

questions.q: Aeroplane skins are inspected on a schedule to find cracks. What principle is this?
o: Damage tolerance: find cracks before they reach critical size
Safe-life only: replace parts after a fixed time without inspection
Ignore cracks until something fails
Crack growth never occurs in thin aeroplane skins
questions.why: Damage-tolerant design assumes cracks and ensures they are found and repaired in time.

questions.q: Explain why shot-peening a surface can extend fatigue life.
questions.model: Peening leaves a layer of compressive residual stress at the surface. Cracks begin at the surface under tension, so the compressive layer makes them harder to start and slows their growth.
questions.why: Residual compression offsets applied tension at the surface.

questions.q: Match each concept to its meaning.
questions.why: These are core fatigue and fracture ideas.

panel.q: A crane hook is found with a 3 mm crack. The critical size is calculated as 80 mm. Should it continue in service?
o: No: remove it, because growth rate and uncertainty make cracks unacceptable in lifting gear
Yes: 3 mm is much less than 80 mm, so there is plenty of margin
Yes: paint over the crack to hide it
Yes: for ten more years without checks
panel.why: Lifting equipment standards require withdrawal of cracked parts, and the crack growth is uncertain.

panel.q: Aluminium has no true endurance limit. What does this mean for design?
o: Use a fatigue strength at a stated life and assume failure eventually at any cyclic stress
There is infinite life below a stress threshold, as for steel
Fatigue is irrelevant for aluminium parts in service
Use the steel endurance numbers for aluminium instead
panel.why: Aluminium S–N curves keep sloping down.

panel.q: Why does a corrosive environment shorten fatigue life?
o: Pits form stress raisers and corrosion helps crack growth
Corrosion strengthens the metal against cracks
It lowers the stress and so slows the cracks
It removes load cycles from the part and so saves life
panel.why: Corrosion fatigue combines both, with no safe endurance limit.

teach.topic: Why a part can break under a load far below its strength
teach.model: Repeated loading starts a tiny crack at a notch or flaw. Each cycle the crack grows a little, and the remaining metal gets weaker until it suddenly fails. So repeated stress below yield can still cause failure. Designers avoid sharp corners, reduce stress and inspect for cracks.

points.ask: What kind of load causes it?
Where does it start?
What happens as time goes on?
How do engineers prevent it?

stages.title: Advanced machine design
stages.hook: A bolted flange carries a pulsing load. Tighten the bolts more and the joint survives; tighten them too little and the bolts fail. Why does preload matter so much?
explain: Advanced machine design combines the loads on several elements with failure theory. For gears, the tangential force at the pitch circle is Ft = T ÷ (d ÷ 2) and the radial force is Fr = Ft tan φ with pressure angle φ = 20°. A 100 N m torque on a pitch diameter of 0.1 m gives Ft = 2000 N and Fr = 2000 × 0.364 = 728 N. These loads bend the shaft and load the bearings, so shaft and bearings are designed together.

A shaft sees rotating bending and steady torque, so each point sees fully reversed bending stress. Design checks use fatigue criteria with stress concentration at keyways, shoulders and press fits, and also deflection and critical speed.

In a bolted joint, tightening gives the bolt a tensile preload Fi and clamps the members. An approximate tightening torque is T = K Fi d, with K about 0.2 for a lightly lubricated steel thread. For Fi = 30 kN and d = 12 mm, T = 0.2 × 30 000 × 0.012 = 72 N m. When an external tensile load P is applied, the bolt takes only a fraction C = kb ÷ (kb + km) of it, and the clamped members take the rest by unloading. With C = 0.25 and P = 20 kN, bolt load = 30 + 0.25 × 20 = 35 kN. A high preload keeps the amplitude seen by the bolt small, so fatigue life is long. If the external load exceeds the preload-limited limit the joint separates and the bolt takes all of the load.

Design decisions include choosing reliability targets, materials, lubrication, tolerances and fits, and ensuring safety through guards, torque-limiting couplings and overload protection. Typical failure causes are fatigue at stress raisers, under-tightened bolts, misalignment, lubrication loss and wrong assumptions about the load.

example.q: A spur gear has a pitch diameter of 0.1 m, transmits 100 N m, and has a 20° pressure angle. Find the tangential and radial tooth forces.
steps: Pitch radius = 0.05 m, so Ft = T ÷ r = 100 ÷ 0.05 = 2000 N.

analogies.home: A tight jar lid grips by friction from preload; if loose, it rattles and slips.
analogies.city: Bridge bolts are tightened to a set tension so that the plates clamp together.
analogies.farm: A tractor wheel is held by tightened nuts; vibration can loosen them if they are not torqued correctly.
analogies.sport: A bicycle's stem bolts must be tightened to a torque setting to avoid slipping or cracking.

stages.mnemonic: Tighten to preload; the joint carries, the bolt sees only a fraction.
terms: The tension put in a bolt by tightening.
Fraction of external load that the bolt carries, kb ÷ (kb + km).
Angle between tooth force direction and the pitch-circle tangent.
Geometric feature that raises local stress.

misc.wrong: A looser bolt is safer because it is not stressed as much.
misc.right: A properly preloaded bolt sees less variation in stress under pulsing load and resists fatigue and loosening.

stages.limits: The torque-preload relation varies widely with friction, so critical bolts are tensioned by methods that control stretch or tension.

With Ft = 2000 N and a 20° pressure angle (tan 20° = 0.364), what is the radial force in newtons?

Why does high bolt preload improve fatigue life under a pulsing external load?
o: The bolt sees only a small fraction of the load variation
The bolt carries the whole load variation as before
The bolt never stretches under any load
The joint is stiffer than steel itself and so carries nothing
questions.why: The clamped members take most of the cycle, so the alternating stress on the bolt is small.

questions.q: A shaft carrying a gear fails at a keyway after months. What is the most likely mechanism?
o: Fatigue from rotating bending at a stress raiser
Instant overload on the first turn of the shaft
Cooling of the shaft in operation
Corrosion only, with no cyclic stress
questions.why: Rotating bending makes each point see reversed stress every turn, and keyways concentrate stress.

questions.q: A gearbox is rated at a safety factor of 1.2. What is the problem if the design load is uncertain by ±40%?
o: The margin is too small to cover the uncertainty
The margin is too large and wastes material
Safety factors are irrelevant to uncertain loads
There is no problem at all with 1.2
questions.why: Safety factors must cover uncertainty in loads, materials and analysis.

questions.q: Why are some drives fitted with a torque limiter or shear pin?
o: To protect against overload and limit damage
To increase the torque the drive can send
To raise the speed of the output shaft
To save paint on the guard
questions.why: A controlled weak link fails first and saves costly parts.

questions.q: A flange bolt keeps loosening on a vibrating machine. Give two engineering measures to fix it and explain why they work.
questions.model: Raise and control the preload with a torque or tension method so that friction under the head keeps the joint from slipping, and add a locking device such as a locknut or thread-locking adhesive. Reducing the vibration with isolation or damping also lowers the cycle load.
questions.why: Loosening happens when slip reduces the preload.

questions.q: Match each quantity to its meaning.
pairs: Fraction of external load taken by the bolt
questions.why: These quantities appear in gear and bolt calculations.

panel.q: A critical bolt is tightened with an impact wrench to 'about right'. What is the risk?
o: Large preload scatter from friction variation causes under- or over-tightening
A perfect preload every time
No risk at all, since the wrench is powerful
Bolts always self-adjust to the correct tension afterwards
panel.why: Friction scatter makes torque-based preload uncertain by ±25% or more, so critical joints use controlled methods.

panel.q: Increasing the gear pressure angle from 14.5° to 25° tends to do what?
o: Raise radial loads on shafts and bearings
Eliminate radial loads on the shafts completely
Reduce the thickness of the teeth at the root
Lower the torque the gears can transmit
panel.why: Fr = Ft tan φ grows with φ, although teeth become stronger.

panel.q: A designer must choose between a design that is lighter and one that is easier to inspect for cracks. For a safety-critical part, what is a sound approach?
o: Prefer a design with accessible, inspectable critical areas unless the lighter one is proven safe
Always take the lightest design, whatever the access
Never inspect parts that were designed carefully
Remove all margins once the design is calculated
panel.why: Damage-tolerant and maintainable design can outweigh small weight savings.

teach.model: Tightening a bolt stretches it and clamps the joint. When an external load pulls on the joint, the clamped parts give up some of their squeeze instead of the bolt taking all the load. The bolt therefore feels only a small fraction of the changing load, so it lasts much longer in fatigue.

What happens when a load pulls on the joint?
Who takes most of the load?
Why does this help the bolt last?

stages.title: Robotics and mechatronics
stages.hook: A robot arm must place a part to within a fraction of a millimetre, yet its motors only know how far their shafts have turned. How does it work out where its hand is?
explain: Mechatronics combines mechanics, electronics, sensing, control and software. A robot is a mechatronic system: structure and joints, actuators (electric motors, hydraulics), sensors (encoders, force sensors, cameras), a controller and software.

Forward kinematics finds the hand position from joint angles. For a planar two-link arm with lengths l₁ = 0.5 m and l₂ = 0.3 m, joint angles θ₁ = 30° and θ₂ = 45° (relative), x = l₁ cos θ₁ + l₂ cos(θ₁ + θ₂) = 0.433 + 0.3 × 0.259 = 0.511 m and y = l₁ sin θ₁ + l₂ sin(θ₁ + θ₂) = 0.25 + 0.290 = 0.540 m. Inverse kinematics finds the angles for a given position and may have several solutions or none (outside the reach of 0.8 m).

Joint torques come from loads. With the arm horizontal and a 2 kg payload at 0.8 m, the static torque at the base is 2 × 9.8 × 0.8 = 15.7 N m (ignoring arm weight). A motor with 0.5 N m, a 50:1 gearbox and 80% efficiency delivers 0.5 × 50 × 0.8 = 20 N m. An encoder of 1000 lines per revolution gives 4000 counts per turn in quadrature; after the 50:1 gearbox the joint resolution is 360° ÷ (4000 × 50) = 0.0018°.

Safety is a design driver. Industrial robots are fenced or use safety-rated sensors; collaborative robots limit force and speed (ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066 give requirements). Emergency stops, safe torque off, risk assessment and training are needed. Failure causes include gear backlash, cable fatigue, sensor drift, software faults and singularities where the arm loses control in some direction.

For a two-link arm of 0.5 m and 0.3 m at 30° and 45°, the hand is about 0.51 m across and 0.54 m up.

stages.title: Control systems
stages.hook: A cruise control holds a steady speed uphill and downhill. What does it measure, what does it adjust, and why can it overshoot or oscillate?
explain: A control system uses feedback: it measures the output, compares it with the desired value (the setpoint), and drives an actuator to reduce the error. Open-loop control has no measurement, so it cannot correct for disturbances.

A first-order process with gain and time constant τ responds to a step by approaching its final value exponentially: y(t) = y_final (1 − e^(−t ÷ τ)). At t = τ it reaches 63.2% and at 3τ it reaches 95.0%. With proportional control and loop gain K on a plant of DC gain 1 under unity feedback, the steady-state error to a step is 1 ÷ (1 + K): for K = 9 the output stops 10% short.

A PID controller sums three terms: proportional (present error), integral (accumulated error, which removes steady-state error) and derivative (rate of change, which adds damping). Too much gain gives oscillation and instability. Integral action can wind up when the actuator saturates, so anti-windup limits are added.

Second-order systems have damping ratio ζ. The overshoot is exp(−π ζ ÷ √(1 − ζ²)); for ζ = 0.5 it is 16.3%. Stability needs all closed-loop poles in the left half of the s-plane. Safety link: control systems for cranes, lifts and robots must fail safe, with limit switches, watchdog timers and independent emergency stops, because sensor failures and software bugs happen.

example.q: A proportional loop with unity feedback and loop gain K = 9 controls a plant with DC gain 1. What is the steady-state error to a unit step?

Proportional alone
Derivative

No heater is fitted to the control

questions.why: Proportional control alone leaves a steady-state error under constant load.

The delay helps by smoothing the signal
Nothing changes whatever the gain

A bigger heater so it heats up faster

A different setpoint for the oven

teach.model: A feedback controller measures the output, subtracts it from the target to get the error, and uses the error to change the actuator. A thermostat is one. A PID controller uses the present error, the accumulated error and its rate of change. Too much gain makes it overshoot or oscillate.

stages.title: Additive manufacturing
stages.hook: A hollow lattice that cannot be cast or machined can be printed in one go. What does this freedom cost in speed, strength and quality?
explain: Additive manufacturing (AM) builds parts layer by layer from a digital model. Main process families include material extrusion (FDM), vat photopolymerisation (SLA), powder bed fusion (SLS for polymers, SLM/DMLS for metals), binder jetting and directed energy deposition. The CAD model is sliced into layers, and the machine follows the toolpath.

Build time depends on height, layer thickness and time per layer. A 60 mm tall part with 0.2 mm layers needs 300 layers; at 40 s per layer that is 12 000 s, or 3.3 h. Thinner layers give finer surfaces but longer builds. Orientation affects surface finish, support needed and strength. Parts are often anisotropic: weaker between layers.

In laser powder bed fusion the volumetric energy density, VED = P ÷ (v h t), links laser power P, scan speed v, hatch spacing h and layer thickness t. For P = 200 W, v = 1000 mm/s, h = 0.1 mm and t = 0.03 mm, VED = 200 ÷ (1000 × 0.1 × 0.03) = 66.7 J/mm³. Too little energy leaves lack-of-fusion pores; too much creates keyhole pores and distortion. Residual stresses cause warping, so supports, stress-relief heat treatment and sometimes hot isostatic pressing are used.

Design for AM allows topology-optimised shapes, internal channels and part consolidation, but needs support planning, overhang limits and post-processing (support removal, machining of critical surfaces, inspection). Safety issues include fine metal powders (fire, explosion and inhalation risks), lasers, hot surfaces, resins that irritate skin and fumes, so ventilation, protective equipment and handling procedures are essential. AM is most economical for complex, low-volume or customised parts, not mass production of simple shapes.

example.q: A part 60 mm tall is printed in 0.2 mm layers, taking 40 s per layer. How long is the build?

stages.title: Manufacturing optimisation
stages.hook: Two factories have the same machines and the same staff, but one makes 30% more good parts per day with less stock in the warehouse. What is it doing differently?
explain: Manufacturing optimisation raises output, quality and flexibility while cutting cost, time and waste. It starts with measurement. Takt time is the available production time divided by customer demand: 450 minutes for 225 units gives a takt time of 2 minutes per unit. A line must produce at least that rate.

Line balancing assigns tasks to stations so that each has a similar work content. Efficiency = total task time ÷ (number of stations × cycle time). With 9 minutes of work, 5 stations and a 2-minute cycle, efficiency = 9 ÷ 10 = 90%. Overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) multiplies availability, performance and quality: 0.90 × 0.95 × 0.98 = 83.8%.

Inventory trade-offs: the economic order quantity EOQ = √(2 D S ÷ H), where D is annual demand, S the cost per order and H the holding cost per unit per year. For D = 10 000, S = 50 and H = 2, EOQ = √(1 000 000 ÷ 2) = 707 units. Little's law links work in progress, throughput and lead time: WIP = throughput × lead time, so 20 units per hour with a 3-hour lead time means 60 units in progress. Reducing WIP shortens lead time.

Lean thinking removes waste such as waiting, over-production, defects and unnecessary motion. Constraints (bottlenecks) limit output, so improving a non-bottleneck gains nothing. Optimisation must respect safety and ethics: pushing speed or cutting maintenance can raise the risk of accidents and defects. Scheduling and simulation tools test options before changing the factory.

example.q: A factory works 450 minutes a day and customers want 225 units. Find the takt time. A line needs 9 minutes of work content per unit across 5 stations with a 2-minute cycle. Find the balance efficiency.
steps: Capacity of the stations = 5 × 2 = 10 minutes of station time.

stages.title: Product lifecycle and reliability
stages.hook: A pump is rated to run for years, yet the company's warranty data show many fail in the first weeks, and more again after a decade. Why do failures bunch like that?
explain: A product's lifecycle runs from concept and design through manufacture, use, maintenance and end of life. Product lifecycle management (PLM) tracks requirements, designs, changes and service data. Lifecycle assessment (LCA) counts energy, materials and emissions across all stages, so design can reduce the total impact, not just the cost to produce.

Reliability is the probability that a product performs its function for a stated time. For a constant failure rate λ, R(t) = e^(−λ t) and MTBF = 1 ÷ λ. With λ = 2 × 10⁻⁴ per hour, MTBF = 5000 h, and over 1000 h the reliability is R = e^(−0.2) = 0.819. Real failure rates follow a bathtub curve: high early failures (infant mortality from defects), a low steady period, then rising wear-out failures.

System reliability depends on layout. In series every part must work: R = 0.95 × 0.90 × 0.98 = 0.838. In parallel (redundant) the system works if either works: 1 − (1 − 0.9)² = 0.99. Availability for repairable equipment is A = MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR); with MTBF = 500 h and MTTR = 10 h, A = 0.980.

Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) ranks risks by RPN = severity × occurrence × detection, such as 8 × 4 × 5 = 160, so effort goes to the highest risks. Maintenance strategies are run-to-failure, preventive (time-based), condition-based and predictive. End-of-life design asks: can the product be repaired, reused, remanufactured or recycled? Ethics and sustainability require honest reliability claims, safe disposal and fair labour across the supply chain.

example.q: A pump has a constant failure rate of 2 × 10⁻⁴ per hour. Find the MTBF and the probability it survives 1000 h.

questions.why: Downtime per failure matters as much as failure frequency.

panel.q: A component with a constant failure rate has MTBF = 5000 h. About what fraction of units survive to 5000 h?
A safety-critical system uses two identical sensors in parallel. A single design flaw in the sensors can still disable both. What is this called?
o: Common-cause failure
Random wear of one sensor at a time
Perfect redundancy of the two sensors
A delay in repair after failure
panel.why: Redundancy fails to protect against a shared cause, so diversity is used.

panel.q: A company hides evidence of a recurring safety defect to protect its sales. Why is this an engineering ethics failure?
o: It puts users at risk and breaches the duty to public safety
It increases reliability of the product over time
It is acceptable if profit is high enough
It is only a business choice, not an engineering matter
panel.why: Codes of engineering ethics place public safety first and require honest reporting.

teach.topic: What the bathtub curve says about failures
teach.model: Failures are common early on because of manufacturing defects, rare during the main useful life, and common again at the end from wear-out. This shape is called the bathtub curve. Engineers use burn-in tests to remove early failures and maintenance to catch wear-out before it causes harm.
